Concept Notes

Study each diagram alongside its notes — in geometry, the figure is the argument. Every marking (ticks = equal sides, arrows = parallel sides, arcs = angles, small square = 90°) is used in the questions.

1. What is a Quadrilateral? The Angle Sum Property

A quadrilateral is a closed figure made of four straight sides (from Latin quadri = four, latus = side). A figure fails to be a quadrilateral if it is not closed, if a side is curved, or if it has more or fewer than four sides.

Angle sum property: a diagonal splits any quadrilateral into two triangles. Since each triangle's angles add to 180°, the sum of all four angles of any quadrilateral is 360° — this holds even for concave (dented) quadrilaterals, counting the reflex vertex's interior angle.

Immediate consequence: a quadrilateral cannot have exactly three right angles with the fourth angle not a right angle, because the fourth angle would be forced to be 360° − 270° = 90°.

2. The Family of Special Quadrilaterals

Rectangle: all angles 90°.  Square: all angles 90° and all sides equal.  Parallelogram: opposite sides parallel.  Rhombus: all sides equal.  Kite: two non-overlapping pairs of adjacent sides equal (AB = BC and CD = DA).  Trapezium: at least one pair of parallel opposite sides.

Marking conventions used throughout: tick marks show equal sides, arrow marks show parallel sides, arcs show angles, and a small square shows a right angle.

3. Rectangle — Properties and the Carpenter's Problem

Properties: (1) all angles are 90°; (2) opposite sides are equal; (3) opposite sides are parallel; (4) the diagonals are equal in length and bisect each other (bisect = cut into two equal parts).

The Carpenter's Problem: two strips (the diagonals) form a rectangle exactly when they are equal and joined at their midpoints — the angle between them does not matter. Proof idea: with equal bisecting diagonals, each of the four triangles at O is isosceles; adding the base angles gives every vertex angle as (90° − x/2) + x/2 = 90°. This method is used by carpenters in Europe and by house-builders in Mozambique to get true rectangular frames.

Equivalent definitions of a rectangle (all describe the same set): (a) all angles 90° and opposite sides equal; (b) simply all angles 90° (Deduction 4 shows the equal sides follow automatically); (c) a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other.

4. Square — a Special Rectangle

A square is a rectangle with all sides equal, so every rectangle property holds, plus: the diagonals bisect each other at 90°, and the diagonals bisect the vertex angles (each 90° corner is split into 45° + 45°).

To build a square from diagonals: make them equal, bisecting each other, and perpendicular. In ΔADC of a square, angle 1 + angle 3 + 90° = 180° with AD = DC forces each base angle to be 45°.

5. Parallelogram

Definition: opposite sides parallel. Properties: (1) opposite sides are equal; (2) adjacent angles add to 180° (co-interior angles of parallel lines); (3) opposite angles are equal; (4) the diagonals bisect each other — but they are not equal in general (they are equal only for a rectangle).

If one angle is x, the four angles are x, 180° − x, x, 180° − x. Congruence proofs: ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB (AAS, using alternate angles across diagonal BD) gives equal opposite sides; ΔAOE ≅ ΔYOS (ASA) gives bisecting diagonals.

Every rectangle is a parallelogram (its opposite sides are parallel) — a rectangle is just a parallelogram with 90° angles.

6. Rhombus

Definition: all four sides equal. Any angle (below 180°) can appear at a vertex — a square is only the special case with 90°.

Every rhombus is a parallelogram (Deduction 9: the four angles a diagonal makes with the sides are equal, so alternate angles give both pairs of sides parallel). Hence adjacent angles add to 180° and opposite angles are equal.

Special diagonal properties: the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, and they bisect the angles of the rhombus.

7. Kite

Definition: a quadrilateral labelled ABCD with AB = BC and CD = DA (two non-overlapping adjacent pairs of equal sides). It is made by joining two triangles along a common side.

Properties: the diagonal BD through the vertices between equal sides (the axis) bisects ∠B and ∠D, and it perpendicularly bisects the other diagonal AC (AO = OC, BD ⊥ AC). Also, the angles between the unequal sides are equal: ∠A = ∠C. Proof: ΔABD ≅ ΔCBD by SSS, then ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOB.

8. Trapezium

Definition: at least one pair of parallel opposite sides. With PQ ∥ SR: ∠S + ∠P = 180° and ∠R + ∠Q = 180° (co-interior angles).

An isosceles trapezium has equal non-parallel sides. Its base angles are equal (∠U = ∠V) — proved by dropping perpendiculars XY and WZ to the base, which creates rectangle XWZY and congruent right triangles ΔUXY ≅ ΔVWZ.

9. How the Family Fits Together (Venn Diagram)

Square ⊂ Rectangle ⊂ Parallelogram ⊂ Trapezium, and Square ⊂ Rhombus ⊂ Parallelogram. A rhombus is also a kite (all four sides equal certainly gives two adjacent equal pairs), so Rhombus = Kite ∩ Parallelogram, and Square = Rhombus ∩ Rectangle — the only kite that is a rectangle.

Remember the exam favourites: every square is a rectangle, a rhombus and a parallelogram; every rectangle and every rhombus is a parallelogram; every parallelogram is a trapezium; every rhombus is a kite — but none of the reverse statements is true.

Answer Key & Worked Solutions

All numeric answers verified. Congruence proofs show the expected statement–reason chain.

Section A — Quadrilateral Basics & the Angle Sum Property

A1.
A quadrilateral is a closed figure bounded by four straight line segments. A figure fails if (a) it is not closed (the sides do not join up), or (b) one of its 'sides' is curved rather than a line segment. (Figures with sides crossing each other are also not quadrilaterals.)
A2.
Diagonal SM splits SOME into ΔSEM and ΔSOM. In ΔSEM, ∠1 + ∠2 + ∠3 = 180°; in ΔSOM, ∠4 + ∠5 + ∠6 = 180°. Adding all six angles: 360°. Regrouping, (∠1 + ∠4) + (∠3 + ∠6) + ∠2 + ∠5 = 360°, and these four brackets are exactly the four angles of the quadrilateral. Hence the sum is 360°.
A3.
Fourth angle = 360° − (78° + 95° + 112°) = 360° − 285° = 75°.
A4.
Let the angles be k, 2k, 3k, 4k. Then 10k = 360° so k = 36°. Angles: 36°, 72°, 108°, 144°. Since 36° + 144° = 180° and 72° + 108° = 180°, co-interior pairs are supplementary — the quadrilateral can be a trapezium (one pair of parallel sides).
A5.
x + x + 20 + x + 30 + 2x − 10 = 360 gives 5x + 40 = 360, so x = 64°. Angles: 64°, 84°, 94°, 118° (check: sum = 360° ✓).
A6.
100 + 70 + 80 + 130 = 380° ≠ 360°, so no such quadrilateral exists. If three angles are 90°, the fourth must be 360° − 270° = 90° — so a quadrilateral with exactly three right angles is impossible.
A7.
Yes. Join the diagonal from the reflex-side vertex (say BD): the quadrilateral still splits into two triangles, so its interior angles (using the interior angle at D, which here is a reflex angle) add to 180° + 180° = 360°. The angle-sum property does not require the quadrilateral to be convex.
A8.
3y + 60 = 360 gives y = 100°. Each of the three equal angles is 100°.

Section B — Rectangles and Squares

A9.
∠CAB = 30° so ∠CAD = 60°. Since OA = OB (diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other), ΔAOB is isosceles: ∠OBA = ∠OAB = 30°, so ∠AOB = 180° − 60° = 120° and ∠BOC = 60°. In ΔABC: ∠ACB = 180° − 90° − 30° = 60°. Every corner of the rectangle is split as 30° + 60°, and the angles at O are 120°, 60°, 120°, 60°.
A10.
Angles at O: 110°, 70°, 110°, 70° (vertically opposite angles and linear pairs). Each triangle at O is isosceles (half-diagonals are equal). Apex 110° gives base angles (180 − 110)/2 = 35° each; apex 70° gives (180 − 70)/2 = 55° each. Each corner of the rectangle is split as 35° + 55° = 90° ✓.
A11.
(a) Rectangle: second strip must also be 8 cm, and the strips must be joined at their midpoints (equal diagonals that bisect each other give a rectangle, whatever the angle between them). (b) Square: additionally the strips must be perpendicular — equal diagonals bisecting each other at 90° give a square.
A12.
In rectangle ABCD compare ΔADC and ΔDAB: AB = CD (opposite sides), ∠BAD = ∠CDA = 90°, and AD is common. By SAS, ΔADC ≅ ΔDAB, so AC = BD (corresponding parts). Hence the diagonals of a rectangle are always equal.
A13.
Diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so BD = 16 cm and O is the midpoint of both: OA = OC = OB = OD = 8 cm.
A14.
The diagonals AM and PL of quadrilateral APML are diameters, so they are equal (each = 2r), they bisect each other (both pass through the centre O), and they are perpendicular (given). Equal + bisecting + perpendicular diagonals ⇒ APML is a square.
A15.
Join BD, and let ∠ABD = ∠1, ∠BDC = ∠2, ∠DBC = ∠3. Since ∠ABC = 90°, we get ∠1 + ∠3 = 90°. In ΔBCD, ∠3 + ∠2 + 90° = 180°, so ∠3 + ∠2 = 90° as well. Therefore ∠1 = ∠2 (both equal 90° − ∠3). Now in ΔBAD and ΔDCB: ∠A = ∠C = 90°, ∠1 = ∠2, and BD is common — by AAS, ΔBAD ≅ ΔDCB. Hence AD = CB and AB = CD: the equal opposite sides follow automatically, so 'all angles 90°' is a complete definition of a rectangle.
A16.
No. Opposite sides parallel (and equal) defines a parallelogram; its angles need not be 90°. It becomes a rectangle only with the extra condition that one (hence every) angle is 90°, or equivalently that the diagonals are equal.
A17.
In ΔADC, ∠1 + ∠3 + 90° = 180°, and AD = DC makes it isosceles, so ∠1 = ∠3 = 45°. The same happens at every corner: each diagonal makes 45° with the sides — i.e. the diagonals of a square bisect its angles.
A18.
(i) False — equal, bisecting diagonals give a rectangle; a square additionally needs the diagonals perpendicular. (ii) True — the fourth angle is forced to be 90° (angle sum), and all angles 90° means a rectangle. (iii) True — four equal angles summing to 360° are each 90°.

Section C — Parallelograms

A19.
Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to 180°: ∠E = 180° − 40° = 140°. Opposite angles are equal: ∠A = ∠P = 40°, ∠R = ∠E = 140°.
A20.
∠Q = 180° − 110° = 70° (adjacent), ∠R = 110° (opposite ∠P), ∠S = 70° (opposite ∠Q).
A21.
2k + 3k = 180° gives k = 36°. The angles are 72°, 108°, 72°, 108°.
A22.
x + 3x − 20 = 180 gives 4x = 200, x = 50°. Angles: 50°, 130°, 50°, 130°.
A23.
In parallelogram ABCD join diagonal BD. ∠ADB = ∠CBD and ∠ABD = ∠CDB (alternate angles, since AD ∥ BC and AB ∥ DC with transversal BD), and BD is common. By ASA/AAS, ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB, so AD = CB and AB = CD (corresponding parts).
A24.
In ΔAOE and ΔYOS: AE = YS (opposite sides of the parallelogram), ∠OAE = ∠OYS and ∠OEA = ∠OSY (alternate angles for AE ∥ SY). By ASA, ΔAOE ≅ ΔYOS, so OA = OY and OE = OS. Thus O is the midpoint of both diagonals — the diagonals bisect each other.
A25.
Opposite sides equal: CD = 4 cm, BC = 5 cm. Angles: ∠B = 150°, ∠C = 30°, ∠D = 150° (adjacent supplementary, opposite equal). The diagonals of a parallelogram are not equal in general — here ∠A ≠ 90°, so they are unequal (diagonals are equal only when the parallelogram is a rectangle).
A26.
It must be a rectangle. If AC = BD in parallelogram ABCD, then in ΔABC and ΔBAD: AB common, BC = AD (opposite sides), AC = BD (given), so ΔABC ≅ ΔBAD (SSS), giving ∠ABC = ∠BAD. But these are co-interior angles adding to 180°, so each is 90°. All angles become 90° — a rectangle.
A27.
Steps: (1) Draw AC = 7 cm; mark its midpoint O. (2) Through O draw a line making 140° with AC. (3) On this line mark OB = OD = 2.5 cm on opposite sides of O. (4) Join AB, BC, CD, DA — ABCD is the parallelogram (diagonals bisect each other ✓). For a rectangle, both diagonals must be equal: make OB = OD = 3.5 cm so BD = 7 cm too (the 140° angle can stay — any angle works).
A28.
In ΔABD: ∠ADB = 180° − 65° − 40° = 75°. Since AB ∥ DC with transversal BD: ∠BDC = ∠ABD = 40° (alternate angles). Since AD ∥ BC: ∠DBC = ∠ADB = 75° (alternate angles). Check at B: 40° + 75° = 115° = 180° − 65° ✓.

Section D — Rhombus

A29.
A rhombus is a parallelogram, so ∠C = ∠A = 50° and ∠B = ∠D = 180° − 50° = 130°.
A30.
Diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles, so ∠A = 2 × 30° = 60°. Then ∠C = 60° (opposite) and ∠B = ∠D = 180° − 60° = 120°. (Check via isosceles ΔABC: AB = BC gives ∠BCA = ∠BAC = 30°, so ∠B = 120° ✓.)
A31.
In ΔGEO and ΔMEO: GE = ME (sides of rhombus), GO = MO (diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other), EO common. By SSS, ΔGEO ≅ ΔMEO, so ∠GOE = ∠MOE. These two angles form a linear pair (add to 180°), hence each is 90°.
A32.
In rhombus GAME with diagonal AE: ΔGAE has GA = GE, and ΔMAE has MA = ME. ΔGAE ≅ ΔMAE by SSS (GA = MA, GE = ME, AE common), so ∠GAE = ∠MAE and ∠GEA = ∠MEA — i.e. diagonal AE bisects the angles at A and at E. The same argument with the other diagonal completes the proof.
A33.
If diagonal BD equals the side, then ΔABD and ΔCBD are equilateral (all three sides equal), so every angle in them is 60°. Hence ∠A = ∠C = 60°, while the full angles at B and D are 60° + 60° = 120° each. The rhombus has angles 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°.
A34.
(1) Draw AC = 5 cm and construct its perpendicular bisector, meeting AC at O. (2) On the bisector mark OB = OD = 2 cm on opposite sides of O (so BD = 4 cm). (3) Join AB, BC, CD, DA. Properties used: the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at 90° — so each vertex is equidistant from O along perpendicular lines, forcing all four sides equal.

Section E — Kite and Trapezium

A35.
The quadrilateral is a kite: adjacent sides 6 cm, 6 cm at the top pair and 9 cm, 9 cm at the bottom pair (AB = BC = 6, CD = DA = 9), with the 12 cm common side becoming a diagonal. It is not a rhombus because all four sides are not equal (6 ≠ 9).
A36.
(i) ΔABD ≅ ΔCBD by SSS (AB = CB, AD = CD, BD common), so ∠ABD = ∠CBD and ∠ADB = ∠CDB — BD bisects both angles. (ii) Then ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOB by SAS (AB = CB, ∠ABO = ∠CBO, BO common), so AO = OC and ∠AOB = ∠COB; being a linear pair they are 90° each. Hence BD ⊥ AC and AO = OC.
A37.
In a kite the angles between the unequal sides are equal: ∠A = ∠C. So 2∠A = 360° − 40° − 100° = 220°, giving ∠A = ∠C = 110°.
A38.
Co-interior angles between the parallel sides add to 180°: ∠D = 180° − 135° = 45° and ∠C = 180° − 105° = 75°. (Check: 135 + 105 + 45 + 75 = 360° ✓.)
A39.
Since SR ∥ PQ, co-interior angles give ∠P = 180° − 100° = 80°. In an isosceles trapezium the angles on the same parallel side are equal, so ∠R = ∠S = 100° and ∠Q = ∠P = 80°. Check: 100 + 100 + 80 + 80 = 360° ✓.
A40.
Trapezium UVWX with XW ∥ UV and UX = VW. Drop perpendiculars XY and WZ onto UV. XWZY has all angles 90° (co-interior with the 90° feet), so it is a rectangle, giving XY = WZ. Now ΔUXY ≅ ΔVWZ by RHS (right angles at Y, Z; hypotenuses UX = VW; XY = WZ). Hence ∠U = ∠V.
A41.
All four sides are 4 cm — a rhombus. Each triangle contributes 60° angles: two opposite vertices of the quadrilateral keep 60°, the other two get 60° + 60° = 120°. Angles: 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°. (It is not a square since no angle is 90°.)
A42.
(a) Joined on the 6 cm side: all four outer sides are 8 cm ⇒ a rhombus (the 6 cm side becomes a diagonal). (b) Joined on an 8 cm side: opposite sides are 8 cm and 6 cm pairs ⇒ a parallelogram (opposite sides equal; the congruent triangles give alternate angles equal, hence parallel sides).

Section F — Classification, Venn Diagram & True/False

A43.
(See the family Venn diagram in the concept notes.) (i) A quadrilateral that is both a kite and a parallelogram is a rhombus (adjacent equal pairs + opposite sides equal forces all four sides equal). (ii) Yes — but only a square (a rectangle that is a kite must have adjacent sides equal, forcing all sides equal). (iii) No — a general kite has 6 ≠ 9 type sides; rather, every rhombus is a kite, not the other way round.
A44.
(i) True — ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD and ΔAOD ≅ ΔCOB (SAS with vertically opposite angles) give both pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel. (ii) False — a kite also has perpendicular diagonals; a rhombus needs them to bisect each other at 90°. (iii) True — if ∠A = ∠C = x and ∠B = ∠D = y, then 2x + 2y = 360° so x + y = 180°; co-interior angles supplementary makes both pairs of sides parallel. (iv) False — the equal sides of an isosceles trapezium are not parallel; only one pair of sides is parallel (unless it degenerates into a rectangle).
A45.
A parallelogram. In ABCD with AB = CD and AD = CB, join BD: ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB by SSS (BD common). So ∠ABD = ∠CDB and ∠ADB = ∠CBD — alternate angles equal makes AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC.
A46.
Yes. Four equal sides make it a rhombus, so it is a parallelogram: adjacent angles are supplementary and opposite angles are equal. One angle 90° forces its neighbours to be 90° and its opposite to be 90° — all angles 90° with all sides equal is exactly a square.
A47.
The four corner triangles (e.g. ΔCUV) are congruent right isosceles triangles (legs = half the side, right angle at each corner of CASE), so their hypotenuses are equal: UV = VW = WX = XU. Each corner triangle has base angles 45°, so each angle of UVWX is 180° − 45° − 45° = 90°. Equal sides + right angles ⇒ UVWX is a square (rotated 45°, with side = half-diagonal of CASE times √2... i.e. hypotenuse of the corner triangles).

Section G — Diagonal Constructions & Mixed Problems

A48.
O lies on side AI of rectangle PAIR, so ∠OIR = 90°. In right ΔORI: ∠ROI = 180° − 90° − 30° = 60°. Since RODS is a rectangle, ∠ROD = 90°. Ray OI lies between OR and OD, so ∠IOD = ∠ROD − ∠ROI = 90° − 60° = 30°.
A49.
(a) Equal diagonals + bisecting each other + perpendicular ⇒ a square. (b) The diagonals still bisect each other at 90° but are no longer equal ⇒ a rhombus (perpendicular bisecting diagonals give four congruent right triangles at the centre, so all four sides are equal, but the angles are no longer 90°).
A50.
The creases form a rhombus. The single fold is copied into all four quarters by the two fold lines (which act as mirror lines), so the four crease segments are all equal — equal sides ⇒ rhombus, with the fold lines as its (perpendicular, bisecting) diagonals. To get a square, fold the corner so the crease makes 45° with the fold lines, cutting equal lengths on both — then the diagonals of the crease-shape are also equal, giving a square.
A51.
Tie the sticks together at their midpoints — the thread through their four ends now always forms a rectangle (equal, bisecting diagonals). Now rotate one stick until all four thread-sides become equal (check by comparing with the thread): the rectangle has become a square, and the diagonals of a square meet at 90° — the sticks are now exactly perpendicular.
A52.
The four triangles at O are isosceles (half-diagonals all equal 4 cm). For the triangle with apex angle x, each base angle is a = (180° − x)/2 = 90° − x/2; for the neighbouring triangle with apex 180° − x, each base angle is b = x/2. Every vertex angle of the quadrilateral is a + b = (90° − x/2) + x/2 = 90° — independent of x. With congruent opposite triangles, opposite sides are also equal, so the figure is always a rectangle.
